title: The Sharpe Pint: SpaceX Mania, Fed Hawkishness, and the SOTP Trap

opening_mood.text: Morning. Welcome back to the desk after what we hope was a decent weekend. If you spent it watching the rain or dodging the latest political drama in Westminster, you are in good company. Today, we are looking at a massive biotech land-grab, Elon Musk's trillionaire status, a proper regime shift at the Fed under Kevin Warsh, and why that 80-tab Excel model you have been tweaking is actually just an expensive placebo button. Grab a coffee, let's get into it.

content.text: AbbVie's £8.5bn ($10.9bn) Bet on Apogee: Eczema, Dosing, and the Biotech M&A Boom

What happened: AbbVie has agreed to acquire Nasdaq-listed biotech Apogee Therapeutics for $135.11 per share in cash, valuing the company at approximately $10.9 billion. This is AbbVie's largest acquisition since its historic Allergan merger. The prize is zumilokibart (APG777), a late-stage monoclonal antibody targeting IL-13, slated to enter Phase 3 trials for atopic dermatitis (eczema) later this year.

Why it matters: Eczema is a massive market currently dominated by Sanofi and Regeneron's blockbuster Dupixent. However, Dupixent requires injections every two weeks. Apogee's zumilokibart is a long-acting formulation designed to be administered just once every three or six months. If the Phase 3 trials hold up, this massive reduction in dosing frequency is a major shift for patient convenience and could easily steal billions in market share.

The City angle: This is a classic 'patent cliff' defence play. AbbVie gracefully navigated the loss of exclusivity on its mega-blockbuster Humira using Skyrizi and Rinvoq, but they need the next generation of 'pipeline-in-a-product' blockbusters to sustain growth. The deal represents a ~53% premium over Apogee's pre-announcement price of $88.43. It also highlights a blistering pace of biotech M&A in 2026, coming hot on the heels of GSK's $11 billion acquisition of Nuvalent.

What to say: 'AbbVie is paying a hefty 53% premium, but if they can turn a bi-weekly injection into a twice-a-year jab, they will absolutely decimate Dupixent's market share. It shows that despite high interest rates, cash-rich pharma giants are still willing to pay top dollar for late-stage de-risked immunology assets to secure their post-patent-cliff futures.'
SpaceX's First Week: Trillionaire Musk, Index Squeezes, and AI Coding Fatigue

What happened: SpaceX went public on June 12, 2026, in the largest IPO in history, raising $86 billion at a $1.77 trillion valuation. In its first full week of trading, the stock surged nearly 40% from its $135 IPO price, briefly crossing a $2.1 trillion market cap and making Elon Musk the world's first official trillionaire.

Why it matters: SpaceX is no longer just a rocket company. Following its merger with xAI, it is now a vertically integrated technology behemoth spanning aerospace, Starlink satellite internet, and AI infrastructure. The massive IPO proceeds are explicitly earmarked to build orbital AI compute infrastructure to power xAI's Grok assistant.

The City angle: The IPO was structured with a tiny free float of around 5%. Combined with fast-track index rules that saw it added to the Nasdaq-100 just 15 days post-listing, passive index-tracking funds were forced into a massive buying squeeze. However, the stock saw a late-week dip after SpaceX announced the acquisition of AI coding agent Cursor, signalling that even retail-driven momentum has its limits when 'AI acquisition fatigue' kicks in.

What to say: 'The 5% free float was a masterclass in supply-demand engineering. Passive trackers had to buy SPCX regardless of valuation because of the fast-track Nasdaq-100 rules. But the immediate slide after the Cursor acquisition shows that the market is starting to look closely at whether Elon is overpaying to build his AI empire under the SpaceX umbrella.'
The Apple-Intel Alliance: Geopolitical De-risking and the Foundry Fight

What happened: US President Donald Trump announced that Apple has agreed to partner with Intel to design and build chips domestically in the US. The news sent Intel shares surging over 10%, pushing its market cap past $600 billion.

Why it matters: Apple has historically relied almost entirely on Taiwan's TSMC to manufacture its high-end processors. This partnership, part of Apple's broader $600 billion 'American Manufacturing Program' (AMP), represents a massive structural shift to reshore semiconductor supply chains and de-risk from geopolitical tensions in Asia.

The City angle: This is a massive win for Intel's contract manufacturing (foundry) ambitions under CEO Lip-Bu Tan. The US government already holds a 10% equity stake in Intel (worth over $60 billion) through CHIPS Act funding, making this a highly politicised but commercially vital alliance. It poses a direct threat to TSMC and Samsung's foundry dominance.

What to say: 'Apple is terrified of a Taiwan bottleneck, especially with Nvidia and AMD hogging TSMC's capacity. For Intel, getting Apple as an anchor foundry customer is the ultimate validation of their turnaround strategy. It also shows that the US government's 10% stake is actively being used as leverage to force domestic tech giants to buy American.'
Accenture's Historic 20% Crash: A Consulting Wake-Up Call
What happened: Accenture (ACN) suffered the worst single-day decline in its history as a public company, plunging nearly 18% on June 18, 2026, wiping out billions in market value.

Why it matters: While Q3 earnings beat EPS estimates, new bookings fell 2% and Q4 revenue guidance missed Wall Street expectations. Management blamed a $400 million hit from Middle East tensions/U.S.-Iran conflict disruption, but analysts point to a deeper structural threat: generative AI is cannibalising traditional IT consulting and managed services.

The City angle: Accenture's business model is built on selling human cognitive hours at scale. If LLMs and AI coding agents can do the basic data gathering, report writing, and code migration in minutes, the billable-hour model collapses. To pivot, Accenture announced a $4.18 billion acquisition of cybersecurity firms Dragos, runZero, and NetRise, trying to shift to high-value OT security.

What to say: 'Accenture's crash is a massive warning sign for the entire professional services sector. When the world's largest consulting firm sees bookings drop because clients are pausing broad transformation spend to focus purely on targeted AI, you know the billable-hour model is under structural threat. Buying Dragos for $4bn is a desperate scramble to find high-margin cybersecurity work that AI cannot easily replicate.'
U.S.-Iran De-escalation Progress and Oil Price Slump

What happened: Over the weekend, Qatar and Pakistan announced that the US and Iran have agreed on a 'roadmap toward reaching a final deal within 60 days' during talks in Bürgenstock, Switzerland. This follows an interim ceasefire and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, sending Brent crude oil prices down to around $75.32.

Why it matters: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's most critical oil chokepoint. Its temporary closure had sent energy prices and global inflation fears soaring. The de-escalation has triggered a massive sigh of relief in global markets, causing Treasury yields to ease and sparking a risk-on tech rally.

The City angle: For macro traders and asset managers, this is a major regime shift. The 'higher-for-longer' Fed narrative (under new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh) was heavily fueled by energy-driven inflation risks. If oil stabilizes in the mid-$70s, it takes massive pressure off the upcoming PCE inflation readings and could pull back rate hike expectations.

What to say: 'The Bürgenstock roadmap is a massive relief valve for global macro. Reopening the Strait of Hormuz and getting oil back down to $75 completely changes the inflation calculus for the Fed. Kevin Warsh was looking increasingly hawkish, but this geopolitical de-escalation might give him the cover he needs to keep rates steady rather than hiking in October.'
Fed Governor Waller's Stablecoin Blessing: The Dollar's Digital Shield

What happened: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller delivered welcoming remarks at a conference on the international role of the U.S. dollar, highlighting how stablecoins and blockchain-based financial infrastructure are transforming payment systems and foreign exchange markets.

Why it matters: Rather than viewing stablecoins as a threat to the greenback, Waller suggested that dollar-backed stablecoins might actually reinforce the dollar's global dominance by extending access to dollar-denominated instruments worldwide. He also noted that stablecoin flows create a direct link to the U.S. Treasury market, acting as a new channel for global liquidity demand.

The City angle: This is a significant rhetorical shift from a key Fed governor. For asset managers and fintechs building decentralized finance (DeFi) or cross-border payment rails, this is a green light. It suggests the Fed is increasingly comfortable with stablecoins as long as they are backed by U.S. safe assets (Treasuries), effectively outsourcing the global distribution of digital dollars to private issuers.

What to say: 'Waller's speech is a massive nod to the stablecoin industry. Instead of treating them like a systemic risk, the Fed is starting to see them as a digital shield that locks in global demand for US Treasuries. If you are building cross-border payment rails or tokenising real-world assets, this is the regulatory wind in your sails you have been waiting for.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: After a much-needed long weekend in the US for Juneteenth, traders returned to their desks on Monday, 22 June, facing a complex cocktail of geopolitical chess, a fundamental regime shift at the Federal Reserve, and a sudden political curveball in Westminster. While US futures are trading slightly lower, Asian indices have kicked off the week by hitting fresh records, and Europe is digesting some major domestic political news.
Schrodinger's Strait: Oil and the US-Iran Peace Talks

The biggest driver of overnight sentiment remains the fragile peace process between the US and Iran. Over the weekend, we had a classic dose of Middle Eastern brinkmanship. On Saturday, Iran announced it was re-closing the strategic Strait of Hormuz—just three days after reopening it—citing Israeli military actions against Hezbollah in Lebanon as a violation of the ceasefire. Yet, US Central Command quickly countered that 'Iran does not control the Strait,' and shipping data on Monday morning confirmed that tankers are indeed moving through Omani waters, with roughly 2 million barrels of crude transiting.

High-level technical talks are continuing in the Swiss resort of Buergenstock, led by US Vice President JD Vance and Iranian officials. The market is clearly betting on diplomacy over disruption: oil prices have eased, with Brent crude cooling down toward the high $80s. If this 60-day roadmap to end the war holds, the massive logistical supply shock that has plagued global shipping since February will finally begin to unwind, removing a major stagflationary threat.
The Warsh Era Begins: Ripping Up the Fed Playbook

While geopolitics dominates the headlines, the real structural story for asset allocators is the regime change at the Federal Reserve. Last week's FOMC meeting was the first under newly appointed Chair Kevin Warsh, and he wasted no time making his mark. Rates were held steady at 3.50% to 3.75%, but the messaging was a masterclass in hawkishness. The Fed's policy statement was slashed from over 300 words to a blunt 114 words, completely stripping out forward guidance. Warsh even abstained from submitting his own dot-plot projection, signalling that the era of the Fed over-explaining and hand-holding the market is officially over.

The underlying 'dot plot' was the real kicker. Nine out of 18 officials now project at least one rate hike in 2026. At the start of the year, the bond market was pricing in two rate cuts; it is now pricing in two rate hikes—a massive 100-basis-point swing in expectations. The 2-Year US Treasury yield, which entered the year at 3.48%, is now hovering around 4.21%. This 'higher-for-longer' (or rather, 'higher-for-even-longer') reality is a direct challenge to equity valuations, particularly for debt-dependent tech firms funding the massive AI data centre build-out.
Starmer Steps Down and the Cross-Asset Read

Closer to home, European markets are dealing with their own drama. The FTSE 100 edged down slightly to 10,360.01 following the shock announcement that Prime Minister Keir Starmer is stepping down as Labour leader and will leave office within weeks. While the UK political transition is expected to be orderly, it adds a layer of domestic uncertainty that has kept sterling slightly on the defensive, with the Euro trading at $1.1457 and the US Dollar gaining ground.

Meanwhile, in FX land, the greenback continues to flex its muscles, pushing USD/JPY up to 161.74. This weaker Yen has acted as a massive tailwind for Japanese exporters, helping Tokyo's Nikkei index climb to new record highs overnight alongside South Korea's Kospi.
The Under-the-Hood View

What is the market actually telling us here? We are transitioning from a regime of 'geopolitical panic + dovish Fed hopes' to 'geopolitical relief + hawkish Fed reality.' If the Strait of Hormuz remains open and oil continues to slide, it will take the sting out of headline inflation. However, with Kevin Warsh at the helm, the Fed is no longer in the business of rescuing equity markets at the first sign of trouble. Investors are now highly dependent on hard economic data rather than central bank hints. All eyes are on this Thursday's US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) print—the Fed's preferred inflation gauge—which will provide the first real test of this new, unguided market environment.

content.text: The Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) Trap and the Conglomerate Discount

If you spend any time reading activist hedge fund pitch decks or investment banking pitch books, you will eventually run into a Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) valuation. It is the ultimate weapon of the activist investor. The pitch is always the same: 'Look at this bloated conglomerate. If we chop it up into pieces, the market will value each piece properly, and we will all get rich.' But in the real world, SOTP valuations are often a beautiful theory ruined by ugly reality.
The Core Concept: Why Conglomerates Trade at a Discount

A conglomerate discount (or diversification discount) occurs when the stock market values a diversified group of businesses at less than the sum of its individual parts. Historically, conglomerates were highly popular—think General Electric in its prime. The theory was that a central management team could allocate capital better than the market, and diversification would smooth out earnings. Today, the market hates them. This discount typically exists for three reasons:

items: Inefficient Capital Allocation: Management often takes cash generated by a high-performing, cash-cow division and pours it into a low-return, pet-project division (classic 'empire building').
Lack of Focus: A management team running both a software business and a chemical plant is unlikely to be world-class at either.

The Blended Multiple Drag: Public market investors prefer 'pure plays'. If a company is a mix of high-growth tech and low-growth manufacturing, institutional investors who only want tech won't buy it, and value investors who only want manufacturing won't buy it either. The market ends up applying a low, blended multiple to the whole thing.

content.text: A Simple Example: MegaCorp's Hidden Value
Let's look at a fictional UK conglomerate, MegaCorp plc. It has two divisions:

items: Division A (Legacy Manufacturing): Generates £100m of EBITDA. Peer companies trade at an EV/EBITDA multiple of 6.0x. Implied Enterprise Value (EV) = £600m.
Division B (High-Growth SaaS): Generates £50m of EBITDA. Peer SaaS companies trade at 20.0x EBITDA. Implied EV = £1,000m.

content.text: If you sum the parts, MegaCorp's total implied Enterprise Value is £1,600m. Subtract £200m of net debt, and you get an implied SOTP Equity Value of £1,400m.

However, because MegaCorp is viewed as a clunky, unfocused conglomerate, the market values the entire business at a blended multiple of just 8.0x on its total £150m EBITDA. This gives MegaCorp a market Enterprise Value of £1,200m. After subtracting the £200m debt, the market cap is £1,000m.

The difference between the SOTP equity value (£1,400m) and the actual market cap (£1,000m) is £400m. That is a 28.6% conglomerate discount. An activist investor looking at this would immediately start salivating, buying up shares, and drafting a letter to the board demanding a spin-off of the SaaS division.
Why This Matters in Asset Management and Private Equity

For public equity analysts, identifying a conglomerate discount is step one of a classic break-up thesis. If you can find a company trading at a massive discount where management is actually planning a spin-off or carve-out (such as General Electric's historic three-way split completed in 2024, or KBR Inc.'s potential restructuring), you can capture massive upside as the discount closes. In private equity, the SOTP framework is used for 'buy-and-build' or 'carve-out' strategies, where you buy a neglected division of a conglomerate, clean it up, and sell it as a standalone pure-play at a much higher multiple.
The Common Beginner Mistake: The SOTP Trap

The biggest mistake junior analysts make is assuming that a conglomerate discount is an automatic 'buy' signal. It isn't. It is often a value trap. Unless there is a concrete catalyst to realise that value, the discount can persist—or even widen—indefinitely. You must ask yourself: why would management agree to break up their empire? Executives are paid based on the size of the company they manage; shrinking the company often means shrinking their own prestige and paychecks. Furthermore, SOTP models often ignore 'corporate drag'—the central HQ costs, legal fees, and tax leakages that occur when you actually try to separate the businesses.
How This Links to Interviews
If you are interviewing for an investment banking, private equity, or asset management role, you are highly likely to get asked about SOTP. Here is how to handle it:

items: The 'How to Value' Question: If asked how to value a company with highly diverse segments, don't just say 'DCF'. Start with: 'I would use a Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) analysis because a single blended multiple would obscure the different growth and risk profiles of the individual business units.'

The 'Conglomerate Discount' Question: Be prepared to explain why the discount exists (capital allocation, lack of focus, investor base mismatch) and how to release it (spin-offs, carve-outs, asset sales).

The 'SOTP Trap' Nuance: Stand out by pointing out the practical hurdles. Mention that you must adjust for unallocated corporate overhead, tax friction upon separation, and—most importantly—the presence of a catalyst (like an activist shareholder or a change in management incentives).

content.text: What to Say Over a Pint

'SOTP is the ultimate paper-wealth metric. It's easy to show 40% upside by slapping a SaaS multiple on a tiny division, but unless you have an activist like Elliott holding a gun to management's head, that discount is just the price of empire-building. You aren't buying cheap assets; you're just paying for a permanent holding company tax.'

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: Quant / AI Finance Idea: PatchTST & The Oxford-Man Benchmark

If you have ever tried to throw a vanilla Transformer at financial time series, you probably ended up with a model that overfits faster than a junior analyst on their first backtest. The problem is that standard Transformers look at individual time steps (point-wise attention). In finance, a single daily return is mostly noise; it has no 'semantic' meaning on its own. To make matters worse, attention complexity scales quadratically with sequence length, meaning you cannot feed the model a long historical look-back window without melting your GPUs.

Enter PatchTST (Patch Time Series Transformer), originally proposed in the ICLR 2023 paper 'A Time Series is Worth 64 Words'. It fixes these issues with two elegant design choices: Patching and Channel-Independence. Instead of treating each time step as a token, it groups adjacent time steps into 'patches' (similar to how Vision Transformers group pixels). It then treats each asset or feature as an independent channel, sharing the same Transformer weights across all of them to prevent cross-channel noise from muddying the waters.

Why does this matter right now? A March 2026 paper from the Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance ('Deep Learning for Financial Time Series: A Large-Scale Benchmark of Risk-Adjusted Performance') put modern deep learning architectures to the test on a massive daily futures dataset. They bypassed standard price forecasting and trained models to directly optimise the Sharpe ratio. The verdict? While hybrid models like VSN+LSTM took the crown for raw Sharpe, combinations like LSTM+PatchTST exhibited superior downside-adjusted characteristics (Sortino and Max Drawdown), proving that patch-based representations are incredibly robust when the market turns sour.
The Mechanics of Patching

By grouping time steps into patches of length P with a stride S, we preserve local temporal patterns (the 'shape' of the trend) inside the patch embedding. Crucially, this reduces the input sequence length from L to approximately L/P. Because self-attention complexity is quadratic, this simple trick reduces memory and compute usage by a factor of P squared, allowing your model to look much further back into market history.

import numpy as np

def create_patches(x, patch_len, stride):
    """
    Splits a 1D time series into overlapping patches.
    """
    seq_len = len(x)
    patches = []
    for i in range(0, seq_len - patch_len + 1, stride):
        patches.append(x[i : i + patch_len])
    return np.array(patches)

# 10 days of asset returns
returns = np.array([0.01, -0.02, 0.015, 0.03, -0.01, 0.005, 0.02, -0.015, 0.01, 0.02])
# Patch into 3-day windows with a stride of 2
patches = create_patches(returns, patch_len=3, stride=2)
How to Use This in a Conversation (or Interview)

Next time a colleague or interviewer boasts about using a standard Transformer (like GPT or Informer) for stock prediction, you can gently steer them right: 'Vanilla Transformers struggle with financial data because point-wise attention gets bogged down in daily noise. A better approach is PatchTST. By patching the time series, you preserve local temporal semantics and quadratically reduce attention complexity. Plus, using channel-independence acts as a powerful regulariser, stopping the model from overfitting to spurious cross-asset correlations.'
The Catch (Caveats)

items: No Cross-Asset Correlation: Because vanilla PatchTST is strictly channel-independent, it cannot learn lead-lag relationships or systemic correlations between different assets during the temporal attention phase. If you are trading pairs or index arbitrage, you will need a hybrid model (like CT-PatchTST or adding a cross-channel convolution layer) to capture those dynamics.

Look-back Sensitivity: The choice of patch length and stride is a highly sensitive hyperparameter. Get it wrong, and you either smooth out vital high-frequency signals or fail to capture the macro trend.

Transaction Costs: While deep representation models like PatchTST find highly profitable structures, the Oxford-Man benchmark notes that transaction costs can eat these strategies alive. You must pair them with turnover regularisation or use models like xLSTM which show higher breakeven transaction cost buffers.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Ultimate Reality Check on AI in Systematic Investing

If you are tired of the endless LinkedIn hype claiming that 'ChatGPT picked ten stocks and beat the S&P 500,' this paper is the perfect antidote. Written by Weilong Fu of Columbia University, 'The New Quant: A Survey of Large Language Models in Financial Prediction and Trading' is a comprehensive, sober, and highly technical synthesis of over 50 primary studies. It outlines exactly how sophisticated quant shops are actually integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into their investment pipelines—not as black-box magic, but as structured reasoning engines that compose with, rather than replace, classical portfolio theory.
The Core Concept: The 'New Quant' Paradigm

The paper defines the 'New Quant' as an investment process where LLMs read and reason over heterogeneous, unstructured disclosures (such as 10-Ks, earnings calls, news, and central bank policy texts), generate auditable hypotheses, and translate them into evidence-grounded signals. Crucially, these signals are then handed off to classical, risk-aware allocation engines. As Fu writes: 'In the new quant, language models do not replace classical statistics or portfolio theory and they compose with them.'
A Task-Centered Taxonomy
Fu proposes a taxonomy of how LLMs are deployed in financial prediction, spanning several key areas:

items: Sentiment and Event Extraction: Moving beyond simple bag-of-words to capture complex market context and corporate events.
Numerical and Economic Reasoning: Parsing financial statements and understanding macroeconomic transmission channels.
Multimodal Understanding: Extracting structured data from charts, tables, and visual financial reports.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Grounding model outputs in specific, timestamped documents to eliminate hallucinations.
Time Series Prompting: Feeding historical price and volume data directly into LLMs to generate predictions.
Agentic Systems: Coordinating external tools like Python interpreters, SQL databases, and calculators for research and backtesting.

content.text: Design Patterns for Faithfulness
To make these models production-grade, the paper highlights two critical design patterns that improve reliability:

items: Retrieval-First Prompting: Ensuring the model only reasons over retrieved, verified documents to eliminate hallucinations and ground its claims in auditable evidence.

Tool-Verified Numerics: Forcing the LLM to use external calculators or code execution to verify any math, rather than relying on its own next-token prediction for arithmetic (which is notoriously bad at basic maths).

content.text: The Pitfalls: Temporal Leakage and the 'Time Machine' Effect

One of the most valuable parts of the paper is its critique of academic backtests. Fu warns heavily against 'Temporal Leakage'—often called the 'Time Machine' effect. This occurs when an LLM is evaluated on historical data but was pre-trained on a corpus that includes the future, or when news and filings are indexed with future-looking metadata. This look-ahead bias makes the model look like a genius in backtests, but it falls apart completely in live trading.
How to Use This at Work

If you are in asset management, quant research, or investment banking, this paper gives you the exact vocabulary to cut through vendor fluff. The next time a vendor pitches an AI-driven strategy, you can ask them two highly targeted questions: First, how do they control for temporal leakage during the pre-training and fine-tuning phases? Second, how do they enforce numerical verification to prevent the LLM from hallucinating financial metrics? If they look blank, you've saved your firm a lot of money.
What to Say Over a Pint

'The real value of LLMs in quant isn't letting them trade directly; it's using them as structured signal extractors that feed into a classical risk-controlled portfolio optimizer. Let the LLM read the 10-K, but let the quadratic optimizer do the math.'

sources.title: The New Quant: A Survey of Large Language Models in Financial Prediction and Trading
sources.note: This comprehensive survey synthesises research on how LLMs are transforming quantitative investing, offering a task-centered taxonomy and outlining critical production challenges like temporal leakage.

content.text: Imagine you are at a craps table in the Hippodrome or a casino in Vegas. You need a high number to win, so you wind up your arm and hurl the dice with maximum force. Next round, you need a low number, so you gently roll them across the felt. It feels completely natural. But intellectually, you know it's absolute nonsense. The physics of a bouncing piece of plastic do not care about your arm swing.

This is the Illusion of Control, a concept coined by Harvard psychologist Ellen Langer in 1975. Langer discovered that when you introduce 'skill-like' elements—such as active choice, familiarity, or physical involvement—into purely random situations, people behave as if they can influence the outcome. In one of her classic experiments, people were offered a lottery ticket. Some were handed a random ticket; others got to choose their own. When the researchers tried to buy the tickets back before the draw, those who had chosen their own ticket demanded four times more money to part with it. They genuinely believed their active choice had somehow made the ticket luckier.
The 'Placebo Buttons' of the City

In the City, we are surrounded by sophisticated versions of Langer's lottery tickets. We hate randomness and uncertainty, so we build elaborate rituals to convince ourselves we are in the driver's seat:

items: The 80-Tab Excel Monster: You have spent three days tweaking the terminal growth rate of a DCF model to the third decimal place, adding complex macro-hedging tabs, and colour-coding every cell. It feels like rigorous risk management. In reality, the investment's success will likely hinge on a regulatory shift or a competitor's surprise product launch. You haven't reduced the risk; you have just built a very expensive placebo button.

The Micromanager's Status Update: We have all worked for the boss who demands daily status updates, colour-coded spreadsheets, and hourly timesheets. This isn't effective project management; it's a coping mechanism. By tracking every minute of an analyst's day, the manager gets a warm, fuzzy feeling of control over a highly unpredictable, multi-stakeholder deal.

Over-trading and 'Gut Feel': In markets, the illusion of control is what drives portfolio managers to over-trade. They mistake a lucky streak in a bull market for personal genius, leading them to make increasingly concentrated, risky bets because they feel they have 'mastered' the market's rhythm.

content.text: How to use this at work
Once you start looking for the Illusion of Control, you will see it everywhere—including in your own daily routine. Here is how to handle it:

items: Audit your placebo tasks: Ask yourself: 'Am I doing this because it actually changes the outcome, or because it makes me feel less anxious?' If you are formatting a pitch deck for the twelfth time, you are likely just self-soothing. Stop, close PowerPoint, and go home.

Distinguish between process and outcome: You cannot control whether a client signs a deal, or whether the Bank of England cuts rates. You can control the depth of your preparation, the clarity of your communication, and your risk limits. Focus 100% of your energy on the process, and accept the variance of the outcome.

Ace the interview question: When an interviewer asks, 'Tell me about a time a project or trade went wrong,' bad candidates try to explain how they could have prevented a black swan event. Great candidates show maturity: 'We controlled our process, built in a margin of safety, and accepted that we couldn't control the macro environment. When the market moved against us, our risk limits kept us safe.'

content.text: Don't mistake rolling the dice harder for actually changing the numbers.
